title: Chip Stocks Rebound on CoreWeave Results as Rate-Hike Bets Firm
dek: Tech is bouncing back on Veterans Day after CoreWeave raised its outlook and Nvidia steadied, even as a hot October CPI report left traders treating a December Fed hike as close to certain. The Treasury market is shut for the holiday, so Tuesday's jump in yields, with the 10-year at 5%, stands until Thursday.
quick: Stocks opened higher: the Nasdaq rose about 1.5% early and the S&P 500 about 1%, while the Dow was roughly flat.
CoreWeave jumped about 13% to 15% after beating revenue forecasts, raising its 2026 outlook and reporting a $132.5 billion backlog.
Nvidia rebounded roughly 5% after falling close to 10% to start the week on the probe of CEO Jensen Huang.
Tuesday's October CPI (+0.4%, core +0.3%) ran hotter than forecast, and futures now price a December hike as close to certain.
The bond market is closed for Veterans Day. Stocks trade normally, and no major US data is scheduled.
Brent oil is near $91 to $92 after dipping below $90 Tuesday on Iran deal hopes. Gold and Bitcoin are softer after the CPI report.

blocks.head: Hot October inflation puts a December Fed hike firmly on the table
blocks.what: The Labor Department said consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, against the 0.3% economists expected. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3% against a 0.2% forecast. Shelter, food and energy led the gains, according to BBC and CNBC reporting. No year-over-year rate was published because the BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during last year's government shutdown.
blocks.why: This was the last CPI report the Fed will see before its December 8 to 9 meeting. The 2-year Treasury yield rose about 20 basis points Tuesday, and the 10-year closed at 5.00%. Higher yields weigh most on richly valued growth stocks, which helps explain why the Nasdaq led Tuesday's losses.
blocks.watch: Friday's producer price index, plus a full slate of Fed speakers Thursday and Friday, will show whether officials lean toward a quarter-point or a half-point move.

blocks.head: Fed's Waller backs a hike and keeps a half-point move open
blocks.what: Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in a speech in London on Tuesday that he is leaning toward a quarter-point increase at the December meeting. He added that a half-point move should be considered if core inflation came in around 0.3% again, and that is where it landed hours later. The Fed's target range is currently 3.75% to 4.00%.
blocks.why: Fed funds futures moved quickly. Snapshots of CME's FedWatch tool cited by CNBC and others put the odds of a December hike near or above 85% to 95%, with a half-point increase at roughly 14%, up from close to zero earlier in the week. A hiking Fed tends to support the dollar and pressure rate-sensitive areas such as small caps, real estate and utilities.
blocks.watch: Watch whether other voting members echo Waller's half-point language. He is one of 12 votes.

blocks.head: CoreWeave's outlook lifts AI infrastructure stocks
blocks.what: CoreWeave reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion after Tuesday's close and raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion, above the roughly $12.86 billion analysts expected, according to CNBC. Its revenue backlog rose to about $132.5 billion from $104 billion in June. The stock rose about 13% to 15% early Wednesday after losing more than 40% over the prior month on worries about debt-funded AI spending.
blocks.why: CoreWeave had become a test case for fears that AI data center spending was outrunning financing. A strong backlog and higher guidance eased those concerns for now and helped chipmakers and other AI infrastructure names rally. The Financial Times reported the company plans to raise billions in debt backed by Nvidia GPUs, so questions about leverage remain.
blocks.watch: Rival neocloud Nebius also reports this week, which will offer a second read on AI capacity demand.

blocks.head: Nvidia steadies after a two-day slide on the Huang probe
blocks.what: Nvidia's board opened an inquiry into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, after Huang acknowledged an affair with a woman whom US intelligence links to China's spy agency, according to the New York Times, CNBC and the BBC. Nvidia hired law firm Wachtell Lipton, with former acting US attorney Joon Kim leading the review. The company says Huang remains CEO. The stock fell nearly 10% over Monday and Tuesday and rose about 5% early Wednesday.
blocks.why: Nvidia is one of the largest weights in the S&P 500, so its swings move the major indexes on their own. Investors are weighing leadership risk, possible scrutiny from Congress over chip sales to China, and the lack of a clear successor, all against demand for its products that remains strong.
blocks.watch: Watch for statements from the board or from the House China committee, whose chairman said he expects answers.

blocks.head: Anthropic sets terms for what could be a record IPO
blocks.what: Claude maker Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 a share for its initial public offering, valuing it at about $1.3 trillion, according to the Wall Street Journal and BBC. The New York Times put the top of the range at up to $1.4 trillion. Trading is expected to start around November 19, according to CNBC's sources. The NYT reported that Nvidia plans to invest $10 billion alongside the offering, and the WSJ reported that TSMC approved up to $1 billion for stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI.
blocks.why: A listing this size will soak up investor cash and act as a gauge of appetite for AI after a shaky month for the sector. Large shareholders Amazon and Alphabet could see big gains on paper, the NYT noted.
blocks.watch: Watch for any change to the price range and early order-book reports as the roadshow continues.

blocks.head: Oil retreats on Iran diplomacy and US-China talk stays cautious
blocks.what: Brent crude settled down 1.2% at $91.49 Tuesday and briefly slipped below $90 for the first time since August on hopes for a US-Iran agreement, CNBC reported. That leaves it more than $20 below its late-October level near $113, according to the NYT. Separately, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington and Beijing should hold no illusions as they both cooperate and compete on AI, CNBC reported.
blocks.why: Lower oil eases one source of inflation pressure, and US gasoline has fallen below $4 a gallon for the first time since July. That offers some offset to the hot CPI data. Energy shares are sensitive to any reversal in the Iran talks.
blocks.watch: Headlines from the Iran negotiations remain the main swing factor for crude.

blocks.text: Asia

Asia mostly rose as AI chip stocks rebounded, despite Wall Street's slip on Tuesday. Japan's Nikkei 225 gained about 1.3% to roughly 61,250, its third straight gain. South Korea led the region: the Kospi rose more than 2%, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix up sharply, according to regional market reports. Hong Kong was the exception, as the Hang Seng fell about 0.8% to near 24,350. Mainland China's Shanghai Composite edged up about 0.5%. Asian bond yields rose as traders priced in a higher chance of a Fed hike next month, the WSJ reported.
Europe

European shares are trading near record territory. The Stoxx 600 rose 0.4% Tuesday to about 659, less than 0.3% below its August high, helped by lower oil prices. Early Wednesday, the Euro Stoxx 50 was up close to 0.8%, while London's FTSE 100 gave back most of its early gain. Lower energy costs are a particular tailwind for Europe, which imports most of its oil and gas.
Currencies

Currency moves were small in early Wednesday trading. The dollar index sat near 102.3, little changed, as Tuesday's rise in hike expectations was largely already in the price. The euro held around $1.116 and the pound around $1.334. The yen stayed weak near 158.8 per dollar because the gap between US and Japanese rates continues to favor the dollar. China's yuan was steady around 6.67 per dollar.

US markets are open. Stocks started higher, led by tech. Early readings from Yahoo Finance and others had the S&P 500 up about 0.9% to 1%, near 7,590, the Nasdaq Composite up about 1.5% to 1.6%, and the Dow roughly flat, between down 0.1% and up 0.2%. That partly reverses Tuesday's CPI-driven decline, when the S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,520.93, the Nasdaq lost 0.7% and the Dow shed about 158 points. The S&P 500 is up about 9.5% for the year.

The rally is concentrated in semiconductors and AI infrastructure, while the Dow, which has less tech exposure, is lagging. Trading volume may be lighter than usual with the bond market closed and banks shut for Veterans Day. The VIX ended Tuesday near 19.5, a moderate level suggesting investors remain cautious rather than fearful.

The Treasury cash market is closed for Veterans Day, so yields stay at Tuesday's close until trading resumes Thursday. Tuesday's moves were large. The 2-year yield jumped about 20 basis points to 4.75%, the 10-year rose about 14 basis points to 5.00%, and the 30-year added about 10 basis points to 5.36%.

Because short-term yields rose more than long-term ones, the curve flattened. The gap between the 2-year and 10-year narrowed to about 25 basis points from roughly 31. That pattern usually means markets expect tighter Fed policy in the near term. A 10-year at 5% matters well beyond bonds, since it feeds into mortgage rates, corporate borrowing costs and how investors value stocks.

On the Fed itself, Waller's speech set the tone: he leans toward a quarter-point hike in December and is open to a half point. Fed funds futures, as tracked by CME's FedWatch tool, imply a December hike is highly likely, with readings of about 85% to 95%+ depending on the snapshot. Pricing for a half-point move was around 14%. Not everyone agrees: some portfolio managers and strategists quoted by MarketWatch and Benzinga argue the Fed should hold off on further increases. The Fed's own guidance will come from the long list of officials speaking later this week.
Fed speakers today

items: Thursday: Hammack, Barr, Goolsbee, Daly, Schmid, and Williams in the evening.
Friday: Collins, Logan, Bowman and Daly. Jefferson speaks Thursday evening ET.

blocks.text: Tuesday's sectors

Technology was by far the weakest S&P 500 sector Tuesday, down about 1.2%, as Nvidia extended its slide and rising yields hit high-valuation stocks. Financials led, up about 0.5%, since banks can benefit from higher rates. Energy, communication services and health care also gained. Rate-sensitive utilities and real estate slipped slightly. CNBC described the pattern as a shift toward defensive stocks over the past few sessions.
Today's movers

items: CoreWeave: up about 13% to 15% on a revenue beat, raised 2026 guidance and a $132.5 billion backlog.
Nvidia: up about 5%, rebounding after nearly 10% of losses over two sessions tied to the Huang probe.
Chipmakers broadly: semiconductor stocks rallied premarket alongside Nvidia, as CoreWeave's results eased AI demand worries.
Riskified: rose before the open after reporting third-quarter results.
AMD: MarketWatch reported its shares faded Tuesday as investors questioned whether Nvidia's turmoil would actually move customers to rival suppliers.

blocks.text: Today's moves mostly reverse the AI-related selling. Whether the rebound lasts may depend more on Thursday's reopening of the bond market than on company news.
Oil

Crude is holding near its lowest levels since August. Brent settled at $91.49 and WTI at $86.04 Tuesday. Early Wednesday, Brent traded around $92 and WTI around $85.50 to $86, with FXStreet noting growing doubts among traders about the Middle East peace talks. The broader trend is down: Brent has fallen more than $20 since late October as the prospect of a US-Iran deal improved. The EIA weekly inventory report moves to Thursday because of the holiday, and forecasts call for a small draw.
Gold

Spot gold traded around $4,035 to $4,045 an ounce Wednesday morning, according to CNBC and other price trackers, after falling about 2.5% on Tuesday's inflation data. Gold earns no interest, so expectations of higher rates and a firm 10-year yield tend to weigh on it.
Crypto

Bitcoin traded around $73,000 to $74,000, near the low end of its recent range and down about 2% to 3% over 24 hours by some measures, as Fed hike bets pushed down speculative assets. Ether was around $2,060. Crypto has tended to track the Nasdaq and rate expectations closely, so a tech rebound offers some support while higher yields work against it.

It's a quiet day for data. Veterans Day is a federal holiday, so the bond market and banks are closed while the stock market trades normally. No major US economic releases or Fed speeches are scheduled. Markets will focus on earnings reactions and the AI trade.

items: No tier-one US data today. Several releases, including weekly jobless claims and EIA crude inventories, shift to Thursday.
Treasury market: closed. Cash bond trading resumes Thursday morning.
Overseas: Asian and European markets are open as normal.

rows: Stock reaction to raised guidance and the $132.5B backlog; details of GPU-backed debt plans
Royalty revenue as gold holds above $4,000; guidance
Expected EPS about $1.32 on revenue near $18.1B; AI networking orders and gross margins

blocks.text: Most of this week's earnings news comes from AI infrastructure, with Cisco on Thursday as the next large-cap test. Options pricing implies a move of close to 10% in either direction for Cisco after its report, according to Simply Wall St.

The rest of the week centers on inflation and the Fed. Thursday brings a lot at once: Treasury trading resumes after the holiday, weekly jobless claims are forecast at about 194,000 versus 189,000 last week, existing home sales are expected to slip to about 3.89 million, the government sells 30-year bonds, and six Fed officials speak, ending with New York Fed President Williams in the evening. Cisco reports after the close. Friday's producer price index is the week's biggest data point. Economists expect a 0.4% rise in headline PPI after September's 1.3% jump, with core PPI at 0.3% after 0.7%. Collins, Logan, Bowman and Daly speak that day. Next week, Anthropic's IPO, expected to start trading around November 19, will be a major test of investor demand for AI.

bottom_line: Tech is rebounding on CoreWeave's results and Nvidia's steadier footing, but a December rate hike now looks close to certain and the 10-year yield sits at 5%. Thursday's bond market reopening and Friday's PPI will show whether the bounce can last.
